sweep_summary: Tachelhit (tach1250) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant on Applegate 1958. None of the seven title-works with stress in the title is about word stress: Boukous 1987/1990a/1990b are prosodic-domain phonology (syllabification, sandhi, pharyngealization spreading; theses.fr abstract read, full text not online; the EDB 7 article has DOI 10.3917/edb.007.0068 but Cairn could not be reached by automated download to every download), Jebbour 1996 (two duplicate Glottolog records) and Moktadir 1989 are prosodic-morphology theses from Rabat with no online copy, and Iazzi 1991 concerns Central Atlas Tamazight (Aït Attab), not Tachelhit. All are low/none priority. The one new first-hand source obtained is Ridouane 2014 (JIPA Illustration, open PDF from Cambridge Core, saved with text layer and logged): p.218 'Tashlhiyt has no lexical stress (Applegate 1958)', prominence being phrase-level tonal placement - it contradicts the fixed-dominant coding and, notably, reads the catalog's own deciding source as evidence for no lexical stress. This lines up with the held Roettger 2017:58 and Bruggeman 2020:46 verdicts already held by the project; the reclassify recommendation (no-word-stress, or 'conflict' registering Gordon & Nafi 2012) stands.fr, Crossref, HAL, toubkal, Google Books and Cambridge Core APIs directly.

new_statements.reading: The standard IPA sketch of the language, by its principal phonetician, states that Tashlhiyt has no lexical (word) stress and describes prominence only as phrase-level H-tone placement (modality, sonority, syllable weight, rightmost preference). It cites Applegate 1958 - the catalog's own deciding source - as authority for the absence of lexical stress, consistent with Applegate's 'non-phonemic' stress and utterance-final primary stress. Together with the held Roettger 2017:58 ('the general claim that Tashlhiyt exhibits word stress needs to be rejected until further evidence is found to the contrary') and Bruggeman 2020:46 (no acoustic enhancement of final syllables), it contradicts the fixed-dominant (word-final) coding; the sole instrumental claim for word-final stress remains Gordon & Nafi 2012 (intensity only), which did not replicate.

new_statements.quote: Stress and intonation Tashlhiyt has no lexical stress (Applegate 1958). According to preliminary observations from Dell & Elmedlaoui (2002: 14), 'the main pitch event' in an Intonational Phrase occurs near its end, i.e. on the prefinal or final sonorant nucleus. Recent work on tonal placement in the language investigated the nature and distribution of Intonation Phrase medial H tones in declaratives (Grice et al. 2011) and Intonation Phrase final H tones in both declaratives and interrogatives (Röttger, Ridouane & Grice 2012, 2013, see also Gordon & Nafi 2012).
new_statements.citation: Ridouane, Rachid. 2014. Tashlhiyt Berber. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 44(2): 207-221 (Illustration of the IPA).
new_statements.locator: p. 217 (pdf p. 11), section 'Stress and intonation', continuing on p. 218
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's fixed: final syllable word-stress coding (final stress): the source says Tashlhiyt has no lexical stress, with prominence only at the Intonational-Phrase level and not tied to the word-final syllable. It is the same statement already held as existing_statements (same passage); 218 to p. 217 (the section header and the 'no lexical stress' sentence are on the page headed 'Rachid Ridouane: Tashlhiyt Berber 217').
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language has no lexical (word-level) stress. Prominence is a phrase-level H tone: the main pitch event of an Intonational Phrase falls near its end, on the prefinal or final sonorant nucleus; when a word offers two sonorant nuclei, the H tone is placed by sentence modality (questions favour the final syllable), sonority (more sonorous nuclei attract it), syllable weight (heavy syllables attract it) and a general rightmost preference; words with no vowel or sonorant may have no f0 peak at all, or the peak lands on the previous word or on a transitional schwa.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; no word-level stress of any degree is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: Phrase-level H-tone placement varies with sentence modality, sonority, syllable weight and a rightmost preference (p. 217); words without a vowel or sonorant nucleus may carry no f0 peak, or the peak sits on the preceding word or on a transitional schwa-like vocoid (pp. 217-218).
new_statements.identity_note: Ridouane 2014 describes Tashlhiyt Berber generally (the IPA illustration), citing Dell & Elmedlaoui's Imdlawn data for the phrase-level observations. Kossmann & Stroomer 1997 is a family-level overview whose Tashelhit section (pp. 467-468) cites Astukn and Igdmiwn dialect forms and the Imdlawn syllabification analysis. Lamjaimer 1996 teaches the Tashelheet of the Souss region (Agadir hinterland) as spoken to Peace Corps volunteers. Boukous 1987 treats the Tashelhit of Agadir.

readall_conflicts: Among the four works opened there is no disagreement: three (Boukous 1987 abstract, Lamjaimer 1996, Kossmann & Stroomer 1997) say nothing about stress, and the only one with a stress section, Ridouane 2014 (p. 217), states that Tashlhiyt has no lexical stress and that prominence is a phrase-level H tone placed near the end of the Intonational Phrase by modality, sonority, weight and a rightmost preference. That statement conflicts with the catalog record, which codes Tachelhit as fixed word-final stress (final stress, source StressTyp2); it agrees with the existing_statements entry (the same Ridouane passage) and with the previously held Roettger 2017 and Bruggeman 2020 readings noted there. The catalog's fixed: final syllable coding thus still rests on sources outside this list (Applegate 1958's utterance-final non-phonemic stress and Gordon & Nafi 2012's intensity result), not on anything opened here.

sources.citation: Applegate, Joseph R. (1958). An Outline of the Structure of Shilha. New York: ACLS (ERIC ED089543). [catalog's deciding source]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress in Shilha is a non-phonemic feature. The stress patterns may be summarized briefly by stating that primary or heavy stress occurs on the last vowel of the stem, provided that the word had no affixes after the stem. If there is an affix after the stem, and this affix contains a vowel, there is secondary or medium stress on the last vowel of the stem and also on the vowel of the affix. [...] [fn.] It should be noted that the stress patterns referred to here apply only to utterances consisting of a single word. [...] It can be said, therefore, that primary stress occurs only at the end of an utterance.
sources.note: Re-read the text we hold layer: the catalog quote is verbatim (scanned 'Shi Itia' = Shilha). Applegate's statement is stem-final (not word-final) stress in one-word utterances and utterance-final primary stress otherwise, explicitly non-phonemic - which is why Ridouane 2014 cites him for 'no lexical stress'. It does not support a word-final fixed pattern.

sources.citation: Bruggeman, Anna. 2020. Lexical and postlexical prominence in Tashlhiyt Berber and Moroccan Arabic. PhD dissertation, University of Cologne (KUPS 11189; defended 2018).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Abstract: 'Experimental results are interpreted as showing that neither language has lexical prominence asymmetries in the form of lexical stress.' p.46: 'The results from the present experiment could not provide evidence in favour of final stress on the basis of acoustic enhancement: Syllables in final position were not consistently enhanced compared to their word-initial counterparts in terms of duration, intensity or F0 ... These results are compatible with earlier suggestions that lexical stress is absent in this language, and that prominence asymmetries may only be specified postlexically
sources.locator: abstract p.v; ch.3 'Acoustic correlates of word-level stress in Tashlhiyt Berber' §3.5 p.46; ch.9 stress-deafness experiment
sources.note: Nine-speaker production study (ch.3) plus stress-deafness perception study (ch.9) concluding Tashlhiyt has no lexical stress; strongest single body of evidence against our classification.

sources.citation: Roettger, Timo B., Anna Bruggeman & Martine Grice. 2015. Word stress in Tashlhiyt - Postlexical prominence in disguise? Proceedings of the 18th ICPhS, Glasgow, paper 0197.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Abstract: 'Contrary to previous reports on the language, measures of acoustic durations and intensity reveal no consistent prominence asymmetries at the level of the word... We conclude that Tashlhiyt does not show any acoustic evidence for lexical stress and that postlexical events do not appear to be related to lexically determined metrical structures.' §5: 'Despite earlier claims, we were unable to replicate evidence for fixed word level prominence ... providing even more evidence against any kind of lexical word stress.'
sources.note: Direct replication attempt of Gordon & Nafi 2012 that finds no word-level prominence asymmetries; contradicts the fixed: final syllable coding.

sources.quote: Les catégories prosodiques dans le cadre desquelles sont analysées les contraintes phonotactiques sont principalement : la syllabe, le mot phonologique et la phrase intonative. [...] Le mot phonologique sert de cadre à l'étude du sandhi consonantique; en particulier, le processus de dissimilation. La phrase intonative apparait comme le domaine approprié à l'analyse de la pharyngalisation.
sources.note: Full text not online (theses.fr 'accessible: non'). The abstract (read) describes a prosodic-phonology study of phonotactics: syllabification algorithm (sonority; any segment incl. stops can be syllabic), consonant sandhi/dissimilation in the phonological word, pharyngealization spreading in the intonational phrase, plus a morphological sketch. Nothing on accent or stress in the abstract. Ridouane 2014 (downloaded) cites Boukous 1987 only for syllabification. A short accent section inside the thesis cannot be excluded, hence 'low' rather than 'none'.
